class Test_TableData_equals:
    __LHS = TableData("tablename", ["a", "b"], [{"a": 1, "b": 2}, {"a": 11, "b": 12}])
    __RHS = TableData("tablename", ["a", "b"], [[1, 2], [11, 12]])

    @pytest.mark.parametrize(
        ["lhs", "rhs", "cmp_by_dp", "expected"],
        [[__LHS, __RHS, True, True], [__LHS, __RHS, False, False]],
    )
    def test_normal(self, lhs, rhs, cmp_by_dp, expected):
        empty_td = TableData("tablename", ["a", "b"], None)

        assert lhs.equals(rhs, cmp_by_dp=cmp_by_dp) == expected
        assert lhs.equals(empty_td, cmp_by_dp=cmp_by_dp) is False
        assert empty_td.equals(rhs, cmp_by_dp=cmp_by_dp) is False
        assert (lhs == rhs) is False
        assert (lhs != rhs) is True

        assert lhs.in_tabledata_list([rhs, empty_td], cmp_by_dp=cmp_by_dp) == expected
        assert lhs.in_tabledata_list([lhs, empty_td], cmp_by_dp=cmp_by_dp)
        assert lhs.in_tabledata_list([rhs, lhs, empty_td], cmp_by_dp=cmp_by_dp)
        assert empty_td.in_tabledata_list([rhs, lhs], cmp_by_dp=cmp_by_dp) is False

    @pytest.mark.parametrize(
        ["lhs", "rhs", "expected"],
        [
            [
                TableData("t", ["a", "b"], [[1, float("nan")]]),
                TableData("t", ["a", "b"], [[1, float("nan")]]),
                True,
            ],
            [
                TableData("t", ["a", "b"], [[1, float("nan")]]),
                TableData("t", ["a", "b"], [[1, 999]]),
                False,
            ],
            [
                TableData("t", ["a", "b"], [[1, 999]]),
                TableData("t", ["a", "b"], [[1, float("nan")]]),
                False,
            ],
        ],
    )
    def test_normal_nan(self, lhs, rhs, expected):
        assert lhs.equals(rhs, cmp_by_dp=False) is expected
        assert (lhs == rhs) is expected
        assert (lhs != rhs) is (not expected)

Before touching anything, I checked what's actually failing: only 2 tests, both pointing to a real bug in `TableData.equals()`'s NaN handling in `tabledata/_core.py:238-245`. The comparison list-comprehension *filters out* any pair where either side is NaN, so `[1, 999]` vs `[1, nan]` never actually compares `999` vs `nan` — the `all([])` on the empty remainder returns `True`, incorrectly reporting equality.

Deleting or skipping this test would hide a genuine correctness bug (asymmetric NaN handling would report unrelated rows as equal) rather than fix it, so I fixed the actual logic instead — it's just as fast and doesn't leave a landmine in the code:
